summary: Background: Adolescents living with perinatally acquired HIV (PHIV) remain at risk of neurocognitive difficulties, yet access to valid neurocognitive tests is limited in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where most of this population resides. Tests that can be administered by nonspecialist personnel are culturally and linguistically appropriate for SSA’s diverse populations and are brief enough for routine use are needed to expand access, but few such tools exist. Objective: We adapted , a brief tablet-based neurocognitive test battery, into Luganda and evaluated its validity and acceptability for use among Ugandan adolescents with PHIV. Methods: In this cross-sectional validation study, 100 Ugandan adolescents aged 11 to 20 years (50 with PHIV; 50 HIV-negative controls) completed the Luganda- or English-language battery and a commonly used traditional test battery. Participants were recruited from an existing longitudinal cardiovascular cohort at the Joint Clinical Research Centre in Kampala, Uganda. We examined convergent validity with correlations between the 2 batteries’ individual and global -scores, known-groups validity with unadjusted and age-adjusted group comparisons, criterion validity by examining classification agreement between the 2 batteries quantified with Cohen κ, and acceptability through self-reported technology use and ease of use. Results: and the traditional battery global -scores were strongly correlated (=0.75; <.001). Correlations between tests assessing similar domains were generally small to moderate, and were strongest for processing speed, attention, and working memory. Adolescents with PHIV scored significantly lower than controls on global scores for both (=.008) and the traditional battery (=.003), even after adjusting for age. Agreement between batteries in classifying participants ≤1 SD (κ=0.56) and ≤2 SD (κ=0.66) below the global -score mean was moderate, with both batteries classifying more adolescents with PHIV than controls below these thresholds. Although fewer than half of participants (42/97, 43%) had previously used a tablet, most rated as easy to use, and prior tablet experience was not independently associated with performance after age adjustment. Conclusions: The Luganda-adapted demonstrated convergent, known-groups, and criterion validity in Ugandan adolescents with PHIV. By delivering automated administration, automated scoring, and standardized multimedia instructions in the local language on a portable tablet, addresses several persistent barriers to neurocognitive assessment in low-resource settings, including shortages of specialist personnel, the time burden of traditional batteries, and the scarcity of culturally and linguistically appropriate tools. The battery was found to be highly acceptable among adolescents with little or no prior tablet experience. These findings add to a growing body of evidence supporting tablet-based assessment as a practical and scalable mobile health approach to expanding access to neurocognitive testing. Future research should evaluate test-retest reliability, sensitivity to change over time, normative benchmarks, and implementation within real-world clinical workflows.
title: Tablet-Based Neurocognitive Tests for Ugandan Adolescents Living With HIV: Cross-Sectional Validation Study

summary: Climate change and biodiversity loss are global environmental crises driving emerging infectious diseases, including bat-borne pathogens of public health significance: Ebola, Marburg, Nipah, Hendra, classic rabies virus, and Australian bat lyssavirus, as well as the fungus Histoplasma This review presents the evidence on the mechanisms of transmission, impact, and prevention and management strategies relevant to each of these pathogens. Transmission pathways vary between pathogens but often involve exposure to body fluids or excreta of a bat or other infected animal or human. The diseases associated with these infections have high mortality rates, and survivors may continue to experience a range of long term effects, including neurological and neuropsychiatric signs and symptoms. Prevention strategies may be implemented to reduce the risk of zoonotic spillover and human-to-human transmission of these pathogens, including better ecological stewardship, reducing exposure of domestic animals and humans to bats, isolation of infected people, and, where possible, vaccination of humans and animals. The mainstay of treatment for these conditions is supportive care; however, specific drugs are now available for histoplasmosis and Ebolavirus infection. In the face of climate change and further loss of biodiversity, developing more effective strategies to prevent and manage these conditions will be critical.
title: Bat-borne zoonoses: transmission, impact, prevention, and management.

summary:
Objectives

To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of adverse event summary reports for medical devices and compliance of the reports with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requirements.

Design

Cross sectional study.

Setting

The FDA manufacturer and user facility device experience (MAUDE) database.

Participants

All adverse event summary reports filed in MAUDE from July 2019 to June 2025.

Main outcome measures

Identification of device problem codes, appropriate identification as summary reports in the submission form, concordance between the number of events data field and the report narrative, and compliance with FDA reporting deadlines.

Results

6308 summary reports were submitted to MAUDE containing 159 503 adverse events. Use of summary reports increased from 808 to 1757 between 2020 and 2024, a factor of 1.21 per year (P<0.001). Most (91%) adverse events in summary reports were for class 3 high risk devices. Summary reports lacked descriptions of potential device related problems: 57% of reports denoted an "adverse event without identified device or use problem" and 38% of reports selected "insufficient information" in the device problem code data field. Manufacturers incorrectly checked "N" (no) in the summary report (Y/N, reporting yes/no) field for 694 summary reports (11%) and erroneously listed "n=1" under the number of events field for 423 summary reports (7%), causing an undercount of 11 902 adverse events. The majority (55%) of summary reports failed to comply with the FDA reporting deadline of 30 days after the manufacturer became aware of the adverse event.

Conclusions

Adverse event summary reports in MAUDE are frequently incomplete, inaccurate, and delayed. Improvements are needed to ensure timely identification of device safety signals and uphold FDA transparency standards.
title: Evaluation of the accuracy, completeness, and compliance of current summary reporting of adverse events to the Food and Drug Administration using the manufacturer and user facility device experience (MAUDE) database: cross sectional study.

summary:
Importance

Rigorous evidence for inhaled sedation using isoflurane in mechanically ventilated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) is limited.

Objective

To evaluate whether an inhaled sedation strategy lowers hospital mortality compared with usual care intravenous sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF.

Design, setting, and participants

Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025.

Intervention

Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death.

Main outcomes and measures

Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months.

Results

Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups.

Conclusions and relevance

In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04415060.
title: Isoflurane-Based Inhaled Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The SAVE-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary: Single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomics provides a great opportunity to explore the complex cellular contents in different tissues. Here we introduce SpatialZoomer, a spectral graph-based method that applies a set of low-pass filters to efficiently extract spatial molecular features from spatial transcriptomics data at multiple resolutions or scales, including the single cell scale, the niche scale with dozens of closely interacting cells and the domain scale with spatially organized cell contents. The corresponding critical scales can be automatically identified by partitioning a cross-scale similarity map. Results show that SpatialZoomer can identify disease-progression signals at specific scales in Alzheimer's disease and spatial context-dependent cell subtypes in tumour microenvironment. The extracted multi-scale features also uncovered spatially heterogeneous niches in cancer. SpatialZoomer achieves comparable or superior performance to existing methods for single-scale tasks, and it also has the advantages of high computational efficiency and low hardware requirements.

summary: Background: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a rare and progressive disease associated with substantial clinical heterogeneity and high health care costs. While machine learning (ML) has been increasingly applied to predict clinical outcomes, approaches that integrate clinical prediction with downstream economic modeling remain limited. Objective: This study proposes and evaluates an ML-based framework that combines prediction of future functional status with estimation of associated health care costs in patients with PAH. Methods: In this retrospective cohort study, data from 181 patients with PAH were analyzed. A total of 6 supervised ML algorithms (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator [LASSO] regression, ridge regression, k-nearest neighbors, decision trees, random forest, and gradient boosting) were trained to predict the relative change in World Health Organization functional class (WHO-FC) from baseline to 12-month follow-up using baseline clinical variables. Predicted change rates were subsequently converted to predicted WHO-FC values at the 12-month follow-up for downstream health care cost estimation. Missing values in predictor variables were imputed using median substitution. Median imputation was performed before the dataset was split into training and test sets. Model performance was evaluated using Pearson correlation coefficient (r), and error metrics (RMSE, MAE, and MedAE), based on cross-validation and independent test set validation. Predicted WHO-FC values were subsequently linked to externally validated, stratified real-world health care cost estimates to approximate future economic burden. Results: Among the evaluated models, k-nearest neighbors showed the highest predictive performance (r=0.40; R2=0.16), followed by LASSO regression (r=0.30; R2=0.09). Prediction errors were comparable across models. Estimated mean health care costs ranged from US $12,481 to $12,614 per patient per month. Despite a significant improvement in WHO-FC over 12 months, estimated health care costs remained largely unchanged, reflecting persistent economic burden across functional class strata. Conclusions: This study demonstrates the feasibility of an ML-based framework that integrates prediction of functional status with health care cost estimation in PAH. While predictive performance was moderate, the approach illustrates how ML models can be extended beyond clinical end points toward system-level applications such as cost forecasting and resource planning. Further validation in larger, multicenter cohorts is required before clinical or health system implementation.
title: A Machine Learning Framework for Predicting Functional Status and Estimating Health Care Costs in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary:
Importance

Despite growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine, empirical evidence on how clinicians use these tools is limited.

Objective

To characterize clinician use of an AI-enabled clinical information platform, the distribution of use across the clinical workforce, and the purpose of submitted queries.

Design, setting, and participants

This cross-sectional study analyzed clinicians with National Provider Identifier-verified accounts of a commonly used AI-enabled clinical information platform, OpenEvidence, from January 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. A large language model was used to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a stratified random sample of 38.8 million queries.

Main outcomes and measures

The number of active users and clinical queries, the share of queries relative to representation in the national workforce, and the clinical purpose and topic of queries were examined.

Results

Overall, 952 008 clinicians (58.5% female), including 556 200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries during the 2.5-year study period. Monthly active users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703 265 in June 2026, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners (44.5) and physician assistants (44.5) submitted more queries per active user-month than physicians (37.1). A higher share of queries relative to the national workforce was submitted by physicians within a decade of graduation (use ratio, 2.54) and residents and fellows (1.84). Use was also higher than average among physicians specializing in oncology and hematology (use ratio, 2.00), internal medicine (1.88), and family medicine (1.80), but lower in procedural and diagnostic specialties (ophthalmology, 0.23; radiology, 0.24; orthopedics, 0.24). Most queries addressed clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management (33.1%), whereas diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries. Queries addressing topics outside physicians' own specialties ranged from 35% among oncologists and hematologists to 88% among emergency department physicians.

Conclusions and relevance

Over 2.5 years, more than 950 000 US clinicians submitted greater than 270 million queries to an AI-enabled clinical information platform. Use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages and was frequently for treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks.
title: Clinician Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Information Platform.

summary: Background: Social media offers valuable information for public health surveillance, but detecting valid symptom expressions in noisy and informal text remains challenging. Fine-tuned language models can achieve strong test accuracy while relying on spurious patterns, limiting their reliability in real-world applications. Objective: This study aimed to develop a more robust symptom detection model by incorporating surveillance-relevant attributes into the training objective and introducing a counterfactual-based evaluation framework to assess attribute sensitivity. Methods: We proposed a concept-aware learning framework (CALF), which combines multiattribute counterfactual data augmentation with multitask learning. We compared standard fine-tuning (baseline) with data-level interventions, a model-level intervention, hybrid strategies, and prompt-based methods across multiple encoders and LLMs for data augmentation. Performance was evaluated on the following 3 datasets: the MedWeb test using macro F1-score (m-F1), the MedWeb checklist using flip accuracy (FA), and a supplementary test set using F1-score for flu-or-fever detection (f-F1). FA measures sensitivity to surveillance-relevant attributes, and the supplementary test score serves as an indicator for out-of-distribution performance. Results: The baseline achieved an m-F1-score of 0.871 on the test set but a low overall FA on the checklist (FA=0.342). It also has limited sensitivity to recovery status, timing of occurrence, and uncertainty of expression. Compared with the baseline, CALF has a comparable MedWeb test score (m-F1=0.880 vs 0.871; P=.18), but a substantially higher FA (FA=0.830 vs 0.342; P=.001) and supplementary test score (f-F1=0.856 vs 0.797; P=.007). CALF also improved sensitivity to recovery, timing, and uncertainty across pretrained encoders. The gains were generally larger when GPT-4.1 (OpenAI) was used for data augmentation. Under GPT-4.1, CALF often achieved the highest overall FA among encoder-based methods. When Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Alibaba Cloud) was used, an alternative hybrid strategy may achieve comparable or slightly better results. Checklist performance was strongly associated with supplementary test performance (ρ=0.811), whereas MedWeb test performance showed weak association with supplementary test performance (ρ=–0.042). Prompting GPT-4.1 achieved the highest FA overall (FA=0.920) and the highest supplementary test score (f-F1=0.910), but a lower test set score than the baseline (m-F1=0.776 vs 0.871). Conclusions: Standard held-out metrics alone do not adequately characterize robustness to dataset-specific or spuriously correlated features. Models may perform well on the test set while remaining insensitive to attributes that influence whether a symptom mention is relevant to surveillance. The MedWeb checklist complements conventional evaluation by measuring sensitivity to controlled attribute changes and may indicate out-of-distribution performance. CALF improved sensitivity to surveillance-relevant attributes while maintaining strong classification performance, supporting concept-aware learning as a practical strategy for developing more robust encoder-based models.
title: Concept-Aware Learning Framework for Detecting Common Symptoms in Social Media Text: Model Development and Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Pedigree mapping serves as the first step in genetic counseling. Traditional methods relying on manual pedigree drawing and information collection are inefficient and prone to errors. Objective: This study aimed to design an intelligent pedigree mapping system based on a specialized model, intended to automate family history collection and standardized pedigree map generation through conversational interaction, thereby enhancing the clinical efficiency of genetic counseling. Methods: This study adopted a participatory design and iterative development approach. We formed an interdisciplinary team comprising gynecologic oncologists, genetic counselors, AI engineers, and patient representatives. The system was built around a proprietary, specialized large language model for gynecologic oncology, featuring a microservices architecture that included pedigree data collection. Through 4 iterative cycles, we integrated specialized knowledge bases using retrieval-augmented generation technology and applied a novel graph-based kinship inference and validation module. The system’s performance was comprehensively evaluated based on the accuracy of pedigree map generation and user feedback on usability. Results: We significantly improved system performance by optimizing dialogue strategies, expanding the knowledge base, and applying self-developed algorithms to improve data extraction accuracy. The initial database of the system defined 100 core information nodes and matched approximately 800 user expression examples, while the final pilot version of the database was expanded to 245 core information nodes and 2256 user expression examples. Although the AI function was limited in the early stage, the final version of the system demonstrated outstanding accuracy in generating genealogy nodes and relationships. Test users generally gave positive reviews of the system’s innovation, ease of use, and intuitiveness of information presentation, believing it to have great potential in clinical practice. Conclusions: The developed system is an accurate, efficient auxiliary tool, and pilot validation showed promising preliminary performance. After pilot clinical validation, it holds promise for integration into routine clinical workflows to optimize genetic counseling services.
title: Construction of an AI-Assisted Pedigree Mapping System for Hereditary Gynecological Tumors: Algorithm Development and Pilot Validation Study

summary: Background: Clinical Quality Language (CQL) and Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) support executable electronic clinical quality measures. Translating national claims–based indicators into CQL remains challenging because terminology, exclusions, and data semantics require adaptation. To our knowledge, Taiwan National Health Insurance (NHI) medical-center indicators have not previously been represented as an executable CQL library. Objective: This study aimed to develop CQL libraries derived from 39 Taiwan NHI medical-center quality indicator codes and evaluate technical executability and computational consistency using synthetic data and real-world cross-institution medication records. Methods: We implemented 39 CQL libraries across 6 principal FHIR R4 clinical resources using 21 data elements, with documented adaptations where official requirements could not be represented. Compiled Expression Logical Model was executed against author-defined synthetic fixtures. In a retrospective 2-campus study, a separately coded Python implementation and the CQL pipeline computed aggregate numerators and denominators for 20 indicators from the same deidentified records, represented as a long table and FHIR resources, respectively. Results: All 39 CQL libraries compiled and executed against the predefined synthetic fixtures, and their outputs matched the author-defined expected results (39/39 libraries; 136/136 early-refill grace-period control groups). The real-world dataset included 88 patients (Taipei: n=65; Linkou: n=23), 1597 medication records, and 630 visits from January 1 to June 2, 2026. Across the 20 medication-based indicators, the 2 pipelines produced identical aggregate numerators and denominators (20/20), and 7 of the 8 cross-institution drug-class overlap indicators had nonzero numerators. All 2317 FHIR resources passed base FHIR R4 structural validation, and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical mapping coverage was 98.3% (1570/1597 records). Conclusions: The implemented NHI-derived indicator logic was executable and computationally consistent across synthetic testing and aggregate real-world comparisons. These findings do not establish complete fidelity to official NHI specifications. Further evaluation requires expert semantic review, patient-level testing, and execution across independent CQL/FHIR environments. Trial Registration:
title: Implementing Taiwan National Health Insurance Quality Indicators as Clinical Quality Language on Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources: Development and Feasibility Study

summary: Background: Regulatory frameworks such as the Belmont Report, the Common Rule, and the Declaration of Helsinki require informed consent to ensure participants understand a study’s purpose and can make voluntary decisions about their involvement. Regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation [EU] 2016/679), further emphasize that consent must be freely given and revocable without disadvantage. Although informed consent forms (ICFs) are intended to be clear and accessible, they have become increasingly lengthy and complex. Large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to navigate and interpret this complexity and have shown promise in biomedical information extraction tasks. However, their susceptibility to hallucinations limits their reliability in high-stakes settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can mitigate such errors. Objective: This study evaluates the integration of GPT-4.1 with RAG for reviewing data reuse language in ICFs and its ability to interpret complex ICF language. Methods: First, we processed 438 ICFs from different trials, including multiple countries, languages, and versions of ICFs. Using expertly curated prompts, we extracted information about data reuse using GPT-4.1. By comparing the LLM-generated data reuse outputs with human expert ground truth, we evaluated accuracy and the time required to extract information for each ICF. To further validate the workflow, we evaluated an independent set of 488 ICFs spanning additional trials, languages, and regions. During the validation phase, the workflow was evaluated using a baseline assessment (89 ICFs) followed by 3 iterative optimization rounds assessed on 14, 281, and 104 ICFs, respectively. For this cohort, we assessed the correctness of LLM outputs along with the quality of supporting evidence provided by the model. Results: Across the initial set of 438 ICFs, the system achieved 81.6% accuracy. During validation, the baseline accuracy using the preoptimized prompts was 84.0% (89 documents). Accuracy improved sequentially across the 3 iterative optimization rounds, increasing from 82.3% in the first round (14 documents) to 90.7% in the second round (281 documents), and reaching 92.1% in the third and final round on an independent holdout cohort of 104 documents. Ultimately, using our RAG-based approach, the system accurately extracted data reuse information across multiple languages. Conclusions: Our RAG-based workflow demonstrated the ability to effectively support the ICF review process for data reuse and interpret complex consent language, contributing to improved consistency in ICF evaluations for data reuse.
title: Large Language Model–Assisted Review of Clinical Trial Informed Consent for Data Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Approach

summary: Background: Accurate documentation of back pain is essential for effective diagnosis and treatment; however, conventional paper-based methods often lack precision and standardization, limiting their clinical utility. Digital pain drawings can improve consistency and integration; however, the literature continues to report variability in digital pain drawing methods, quantification approaches, body schemas, and implementation. Moreover, open access, anatomically labeled vector assets mapped to clinical terminology remain limited. Objective: This study aimed to develop an anatomically accurate, digitally segmented, open-source vector illustration of a sex-neutral human body (front and back views) for standardized back pain documentation and conduct a user-centered design validation and feasibility evaluation of its perceived usefulness, communication value, and visual acceptability. Methods: An interdisciplinary team used an iterative methodology informed by standard anatomical references to create the illustration, emphasizing anatomical precision, digital compatibility, and interoperability with medical coding systems. A survey-based design validation study (N=298) was conducted in the United Kingdom through the Prolific platform to evaluate perceived usefulness, confidence in identifying hypothetical pain regions (without an interactive drawing task or comparator), aesthetic appeal, and suggestions for improvement. Quantitative results were summarized descriptively with 95% CIs, and qualitative feedback guided final refinements. The finalized illustration was released under a CC BY 4.0 license. Results: Mean confidence ratings were 5.7 out of 7 (SD 1.2) for indicating pain regions using the illustration (95% CI 5.5-5.8) and 5.6 out of 7 (SD 1.2) for communicating pain with health care professionals (95% CI 5.5-5.8). Aesthetic ratings were more mixed (mean 4.3 out of 7, SD 1.5; 95% CI 4.1-4.5). User feedback highlighted the need for improved visual clarity, leading to adjustments in color contrast and anatomical proportions. Aesthetic concerns, including the removal of the areolae and changes to the facial features, were also addressed to enhance user comfort and neutrality. Conclusions: The resulting anatomically accurate vector illustration provides a feasible, open-source foundation for digital back pain documentation tools and may support patient-clinician communication and integration with electronic health records. The design validation study supports acceptability and perceived usefulness, but it does not establish superiority over existing body maps or objective accuracy of pain localization. By releasing it under a CC BY 4.0 license, we encourage broad adoption and community-driven improvements.
title: Open-Source Anatomical Illustration for Digital Back Pain Documentation: Development and Feasibility Evaluation

summary: Background: Clinical temporal relation extraction (CTRE) is essential for reconstructing patient timelines from unstructured electronic health records (EHRs). However, the linguistic complexity of clinical notes and the high cost of expert annotation impede the development of large-scale training corpora. While large language models (LLMs) have transformed general natural language processing, their application to CTRE remains underexplored. Objective: This study aimed to determine the optimal adaptation strategy for CTRE by conducting a controlled comparative benchmarking of LLM architectures and fine-tuning methodologies in both data-rich and limited-data regimes. Methods: We evaluated 4 LLMs representing 2 distinct architectures—transformer encoders (GatorTron [University of Florida and NVIDIA]) and transformer decoders (LLaMA 3.1-8B [Meta AI] and MeLLaMA-13B [Yale University and University of Florida]). We compared four adaptation strategies: (1) standard fine-tuning, (2) hard-prompting, (3) soft-prompting, and (4) low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Experiments were conducted on the 2012 i2b2 CTRE benchmark in both full-supervision and 1-shot scenarios. Results: Recent LLMs combined with appropriate adaptation strategies achieved strong performance for CTRE on the 2012 i2b2 benchmark. In the data-rich setting, the best-performing configuration was LLaMA3.1-8B with quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) applied to the query and value projection layers, achieving a micro--score of 89.15% (0.30). Comparative analyses showed that QLoRA applied only to the query and value projection layers achieved performance comparable to QLoRA applied to all linear layers, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Hard-prompting showed particular effectiveness in the 1-shot scenario compared with standard fine-tuning for GatorTron-Base. Overall, Decoder-based models generally outperformed encoder-based models under QLoRA-based adaptation. However, under the most resource-constrained setting, where both training data and trainable parameters were highly limited, encoder-based models achieved better performance than decoder-based models. Conclusions: This study provides a controlled benchmark for adapting LLMs to CTRE under different data and parameter constraints. Our findings suggest that QLoRA targeting only the query and value projection layers is a computationally efficient and competitive adaptation strategy. Decoder-based LLMs generally achieved stronger performance under QLoRA-based adaptation, whereas domain-specific encoder-based models showed advantages under the most resource-constrained soft-prompting setting. These results highlight the importance of selecting adaptation strategies according to both model architecture and available computational resources.
title: Optimizing Clinical Temporal Relation Extraction With Large Language Models: Comparative Analysis

summary: This letter comments on the systematic review and meta-analysis of large language models (LLMs) in mental health care by Leung and colleagues (JMIR AI 2026;5:e87730). The bivariate meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp adjustments is methodologically sound, and its cautious conclusions are warranted. I raise an unaddressed threat to the pooled estimates: model version drift. Over the search window (November 2022 to March 2026), "GPT-4" did not denote a single intervention; released in March 2023, it was followed by API snapshots whose behavior differed materially, with accuracy on a prime-number identification task falling from 84% to 51% between the March and June 2023 versions. Because the review extracted only model name and model type and did not capture version or testing dates, the estimates pooled under GPT-4 (k=4) and GPT-3.5 (k=4) may each span several substantively different models, and the pooled GPT-4 estimate may correspond to no single system a clinician could deploy. This concern is distinct from the acknowledged limitation that few studies evaluated the newest variants, which concerns currency rather than comparability. I suggest reporting model version and testing date for each pooled study (consistent with TRIPOD-LLM item 6a), examining robustness to version mixing in sensitivity analyses, and qualifying the abstract comparative statements accordingly.
title: Same Name, Moving Target: Model Version Drift in Syntheses of Large Language Models for Mental Health

summary: The proliferation of evaluative approaches for generative AI tools used for mental health purposes reflects much-needed attention to safety, ethics, and emerging risks. However, limited alignment across frameworks complicates comparisons, slows progress toward shared goals, and provides little clarity for regulatory processes. The result is a fragmented field that lacks cohesive guidance as the technology and its real-world patterns of use continue to evolve. This position paper synthesizes current evaluative approaches, outlines sources of divergence across existing frameworks, and identifies shared domains that could serve as anchors for coordinated development. We advocate for a living, flexible meta-framework maintained by a global, cross-sector consortium that can harmonize criteria, support consistent evaluation across jurisdictions, and adapt alongside scientific, clinical, and technological advances. Such a structure can strengthen safety, transparency, and methodological consistency while giving researchers, clinicians, developers, and policymakers a shared foundation for assessing generative AI tools in mental health care.
title: Toward a Living Meta-Framework for Evaluating Generative AI in Mental Health

summary: Background: Poststroke seizures (PSS) and poststroke epilepsy (PSE) are important neurological complications associated with poorer functional recovery, increased mortality, and reduced quality of life after stroke. Neuroimaging plays a central role in identifying patients at increased risk, and recent advances in AI have enabled the development of imaging-based prediction models that may improve individualized risk stratification. However, the current evidence remains fragmented, and the extent to which these approaches are applicable to African health care settings is unclear. Objective: This scoping review aimed to chart the existing global evidence on the development of imaging-based prediction models that can help in predicting PSS and PSE, especially AI-based ones. The purpose was to look into the imaging techniques, computational algorithms, and validation methodologies used and the representation of African populations. Methods: This scoping review was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework, and the results were presented based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) framework. Articles searched using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar involved the application of computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), angiography imaging techniques, radiomic markers, or multimodal neuroimaging techniques in statistical and AI-based prediction models for seizure-related outcomes after stroke. Results: Twenty-three studies published between 2005 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The evidence demonstrated a clear methodological evolution from conventional imaging-based prediction models to radiomics, machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, and multimodal approaches. MRI and CT were the predominant imaging modalities, with cortical involvement, lesion location, infarct volume, hemorrhagic transformation, and quantitative radiomic features emerging as the most frequently reported imaging predictors. Most AI models relied on internal validation, while relatively few underwent external validation. The evidence base was concentrated in East Asia, Europe, and North America, with no eligible imaging-based AI models having been developed or externally validated using African datasets. Conclusions: Imaging-based AI for predicting PSS and PSE has progressed rapidly, but important methodological and geographical gaps remain. Limited external validation, heterogeneous reporting, and the absence of African development and validation cohorts restrict confidence in the generalizability of existing models. Future research should prioritize the development of explainable imaging-based AI models using representative African neuroimaging datasets and their external validation in multicenter studies.
title: AI for Poststroke Epilepsy: Scoping Review of Imaging-Based Prediction Models and Implications for African Settings

summary: D2C7-ATC is a recombinant antibody-toxin conjugate (ATC) targeting wild-type epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mutant EGFR variant III (EGFRvIII). We conducted a single-arm, single-site, open-label phase 1 trial evaluating a single infusion of D2C7-ATC via convection-enhanced delivery in the enhancing disease of 81 patients with biopsy-confirmed recurrent malignant glioma. The primary objective was to determine toxicity and the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of D2C7-ATC. Secondary objectives included describing overall survival (OS) and assessing the association between EGFR expression and OS. The median overall survival (mOS) was 7.9 months among 72 patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type recurrent glioblastoma (IDHwt rGBM), including 35 patients in the dose-escalation stage (40 to 35,032 ng ml<sup>-1</sup>) and 37 patients in the dose-expansion stage (RP2D of 6,920 ng ml<sup>-1</sup>). D2C7-ATC was generally well tolerated, with mainly grade 1-2 treatment-related adverse events (67%). The maximum tolerated dose was exceeded at 35,032 ng ml<sup>-1</sup>, where four patients experienced dose-limiting toxicities, including grade 4 (N = 2) and grade 3 (N = 2) events. Eight patients died on trial; all deaths were unrelated to D2C7-ATC. Univariate analyses identified survival-associated biomarkers, including tumor D2C7 antibody reactivity, circulating cytokines, a tumor inflammatory gene signature and neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes in blood. Notably, patients with IDHwt rGBM with a D2C7 antibody reactivity score of <1.5+ in pre-treatment tumor had an mOS of 17.38 months, whereas those with low IL-8 in post-treatment plasma had an mOS of 16.6 months. These findings indicate that EGFR-targeted D2C7-ATC therapy prolongs survival in a subset of patients with IDHwt rGBM via intratumoral and systemic immune activation. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02303678 .
title: EGFR-targeted antibody−toxin conjugate in recurrent glioma: a phase 1 trial

summary: Background: Telemedicine has emerged as a critical strategy to address health care access gaps in hard-to-reach areas, particularly in resource-constrained settings. While telemedicine services have expanded across India, evidence on post-implementation experiences, specifically regarding the integration of portable diagnostic tools, and the assisting role of frontline health care workers, remains limited. Understanding these sociotechnical dynamics is essential for optimizing digital health interventions in remote areas. Objective: This study aimed to explore perceptions, experiences, and implementation processes of an assisted telemedicine model where frontline health care workers facilitate real-time, doorstep patient-assisted-to-doctor consultations using portable diagnostics and a customized portal among health care workers and patients in hard-to-reach villages of Rajasthan, India. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted in 5 remote villages of Balotra district, Rajasthan, between December 2025 and January 2026, following a 10-month telemedicine intervention. In-depth, semistructured interviews were conducted with 28 participants, including medical officers (n=3, 10.71%), nurses, and accredited social health activists or auxiliary nurse midwives (n=10, 35.71%), and patients (n=15, 53.57%). Cadre-specific semistructured interview guides were developed using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and Technology Acceptance Model. Interviews were analyzed using a reflexive thematic analysis approach, incorporating both inductive and deductive coding approaches in NVivo 15 (Lumivero). Triangulation across participant groups and analytic perspectives was used to enhance credibility and trustworthiness. Results: The analysis revealed that the assisted telemedicine model fundamentally reconfigured treatment-seeking behavior by providing doorstep care, significantly reducing travel burdens, and out-of-pocket expenditures. Frontline health care workers acted as crucial sociotechnical mediators, bridging the digital divide and fostering patient trust, particularly among women and older adults. Health care providers reported increased clinical confidence and workflow efficiency, supported by real-time vital monitoring and cross-verification via digital chatbots. However, implementation was challenged by intermittent network connectivity, diagnostic limitations for conditions requiring physical palpation, and occasional stock-outs of essential medicines. Despite these barriers, the gradual acceptance of the system was heavily facilitated by the continuous engagement and cultural mediation of local health workers. Conclusions: Telemedicine was perceived as a feasible and acceptable model for extending primary health care services in hard-to-reach areas, provided it is embedded within an assisted model supported by trained frontline workers and responsive technical systems. The findings emphasize the need to shift health care policy toward mediated-digital models, formally recognizing community health workers as digital health navigators. Future scale-up must prioritize strengthening rural digital infrastructure and ensuring a reliable supply chain for essential medicines to sustain long-term engagement and health equity. Trial Registration: Clinical Trials Registry—India (CTRI) CTRI/2024/10/076070; https://tinyurl.com/yr952847 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/92996

summary: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial weight reduction and cardiometabolic benefit in randomized trials; however, prospective implementation evidence from digital care models and female sex community populations remains limited. Here we report outcomes from an observational study of 8,127 women initiating GLP-1RA therapy (99.8% tirzepatide) through a structured digital program incorporating mandatory biochemical monitoring, weekly video-supported follow-up and clinician-guided dose titration in the UK. Mean weight reduction was 16.1 kg (95% confidence interval 15.9 to 16.2; P < 0.001), representing 15.5% of baseline weight; 83.1% achieved ≥10% and 22.4% achieved ≥20% weight loss, with consistent responses across age, baseline weight and socioeconomic strata. Among participants with paired biomarker data, mean glycated hemoglobin decreased by 3.3 mmol mol<sup>-</sup><sup>1</sup> (95% confidence interval 3.1 to 3.4; P < 0.001), normalizing in 84.5% of those with baseline diabetes-range values and 96.3% with prediabetes, and lipid parameters improved significantly (reductions in total cholesterol of 0.77 mmol l<sup>-</sup><sup>1</sup>, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 0.61 mmol l<sup>-</sup><sup>1</sup> and triglycerides of 0.47 mmol l<sup>-</sup><sup>1</sup>). Retention was 91.4% at 6 months, with no serious treatment-related adverse events. These findings support the feasibility of delivering structured, digitally enabled obesity pharmacotherapy at scale and provide prospective real-world implementation evidence for this care model. Interpretation is limited by the observational design, absence of a comparator group, self-pay population and 6-month follow-up.
title: Real-world, digital-first delivery of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in women

summary: Background: Clinicians spend a lot of time on electronic health record (EHR) documentation, often at the expense of direct patient interaction. Ambient listening technology uses AI to passively record and summarize clinical encounters. Although early studies are promising, there is limited evidence on system performance in complex, non-English settings. Objective: This study aimed to compare the documentation performance of 3 commercially available ambient listening systems in simulated Dutch-language outpatient consultations by assessing note completeness, correctness, and conciseness under predefined linguistic and interactional challenges. Methods: Standardized audio recordings of 10 scripted physician-patient interactions across 2 specialties were used. Scenarios included multispeaker dynamics (patient companion), conversational disruptions (nurse interruption), evasive patient communication, and a regional dialect (Gronings). Three ambient listening providers (provider 1, provider 2, and provider 3) processed the audio files. Generated notes were divided into 4 note sections: patient history, physical examination, diagnostic impression, and treatment plan. For each system output, each note section was scored for completeness, conciseness, and correctness using a 5-point ordinal scale against physician-developed reference summaries. In total, 8 clinicians participated in scoring: 4 junior clinicians evaluated all outputs, and 4 senior clinicians each reviewed a subset of scenarios. Analyses were based on 351 rater-averaged section-domain scores. Interrater agreement was assessed using Gwet agreement coefficient 2 (Gwet AC-2). System-level technical characteristics were assessed alongside clinical performance to aid interpretation of between-provider differences. Results: Across 351 rater-averaged section-domain scores on a 5-point scale, overall interrater agreement was high (Gwet AC-2=0.827). Provider-level mean scores ranged from 3.82 to 4.26 (4.26, SD 0.73 for provider 3, 4.00, SD 0.90 for provider 2, and 3.82, SD 1.07 for provider 1). Mean scores were higher in otolaryngology than in surgical oncology (4.36, SD 0.56 vs 3.68, SD 1.10). Across scoring domains, correctness received the highest mean score (4.21, SD 0.98), while completeness received the lowest (3.81, SD 0.90). Variation in mean scores was observed across script scenarios. Dialect-containing scenarios had the lowest mean score overall (3.77, SD 1.21), although this pattern was not uniform across specialties and systems. Median summary generation times ranged from 13.5 seconds (IQR 12-15; provider 3) to 22.0 seconds (IQR 18-24; provider 2). Conclusions: Ambient listening systems demonstrated generally strong performance in this simulated Dutch-language evaluation, including under several common conversational challenges. However, mean scores varied across scripted scenarios, with lower scores observed in some dialect-containing and otherwise challenging interactions. Future deployment studies must prioritize linguistic equity, real-world validation of efficiency gains, and evaluation of both clinician and patient perceptions to understand how these systems influence consultation dynamics and care delivery across diverse patient populations.
title: Three Ambient Listening Systems in Simulated Dutch-Language Multispeaker and Multidialect Clinical Encounters: Comparative Study

summary: Background: AI-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSSs) can help primary care clinicians provide higher quality care amid rising case complexity and resource constraints. However, evidence regarding their effectiveness and safety in primary care practice is lacking. Objective: We synthesized evidence on the effectiveness and safety of AI-CDSSs compared with usual care or non–AI-based systems in primary care settings. Methods: We conducted a systematic review following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and reported the results according to PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines. We included experimental and quasi-experimental studies evaluating AI-CDSSs used by health care professionals in primary care settings, compared with usual care or non–AI-based decision support systems, and that reported clinician-, patient-, or system-level outcomes, or safety. An information specialist designed the search strategies and systematically reviewed MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and CENTRAL from inception to June 27, 2025. Reviewers independently performed the selection and extraction processes. Data extraction was informed by the DECIDE-AI and CONSORT-AI (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials–AI) reporting guidelines and the APPRAISE-AI tool. We independently assessed the risk of bias using Risk of Bias-2 or Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, we conducted a synthesis without meta-analysis and explored heterogeneity using an adapted Non-Adoption, Abandonment, Scale-Up, Spread, and Sustainability–informed implementation-context classification. The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251119225). Results: We identified 4074 records through database searches and 12 additional records through citation searching and trial registration checking. We included 14 records on 11 distinct studies, including 4 experimental and 7 quasi-experimental studies. The risk of bias was high in all experimental studies and serious to critical in quasi-experimental studies. AI-CDSSs showed more consistent positive effects on workflow-related outcomes in structured and protocolized decision contexts, particularly for screening, referral, and alert optimization tasks. Patient-level effects were limited and inconsistent, particularly in more complex contexts involving heterogeneous conditions or preference-sensitive decisions. System-level outcomes were heterogeneous, with isolated improvements in service delivery and utilization outcomes. Safety evaluation was rare and poorly specified. Only 2 studies prespecified safety outcomes, and the reported safety information mainly involved technical malfunctions or self-reported side effects. No study reported clinician interaction measures such as agreement with, override of, or reliance on AI outputs. Interpretation of the findings is limited by substantial heterogeneity, short follow-up periods, predominantly high or critical risk of bias, and evidence derived exclusively from high-income countries. Conclusions: AI-CDSSs in primary care may provide more consistent benefits for workflow-related and process-level outcomes in structured and protocolized decision contexts, while evidence on safety remains insufficient to support confident routine implementation. This systematic review reveals an important gap between the rapid development of AI-CDSSs and the lack of robust, comparable evidence to support their reliable use in primary care.
title: AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems in Primary Care: Systematic Review of Clinical Implementation

summary: Background: Voice disorders are common, yet access to timely specialist assessment is often limited. Automated analysis of short voice recordings may support early screening, but achieving robust performance on heterogeneous clinical datasets remains challenging. Objective: This study aims to investigate the impact of synthetic speech augmentation on voice disorder recognition and classification using the Saarbrücken Voice Database (SVD) and to develop an adaptive ensemble with learnable weighting and optional sex embedding. Methods: Sentence recordings from the SVD were used for binary voice disorder recognition (VDR, n=1988) and 4-class voice disorder classification (VDC; n=1199). Two text-to-speech (TTS) models, XTTS and Kartoffelbox, generated 1 synthetic sample for each training instance. Synthetic speech quality was assessed in a blinded listening evaluation with 40 samples per TTS model. Baseline models included support vector machine (SVM), ResNet-18, long short-term memory, and transformer-based architectures, including Hidden-Unit BERT (HuBERT), Wav2Vec 2.0, and WavLM. Ensemble learning and learnable fusion (LF), with and without a sex embedding (LFS), were evaluated using bootstrapped performance estimates and standard classification metrics. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was reported for VDR. Results: In the blinded evaluation, Kartoffelbox-generated synthetic samples were less often identified as synthetic than XTTS-generated synthetic samples (10/19, 52.6% vs 17/19, 89.5%). In pooled original and synthetic ratings, Kartoffelbox showed higher pathological-status identification than XTTS for pathological samples (22/29, 75.9% vs 19/29, 65.5%) and nonpathological samples (8/10, 80.0% vs 6/10, 60.0%), as well as higher diagnostic-class assignment (20/39, 51.3% vs 14/39, 35.9%). Among the baseline models, HuBERT showed the most balanced VDR performance (accuracy=0.85, -score=0.84). Kartoffelbox-based augmentation further improved performance, with HuBERT achieving 0.88 sensitivity, 0.87 accuracy, and 0.85 -score. LF showed minor improvements in threshold-dependent metrics (accuracy=0.87, -score=0.86), while LFS further balanced sensitivity and specificity (accuracy=0.88, AUC=0.92). The equal-weight ensemble achieved the highest AUC among ensemble approaches (AUC=0.93). For VDC, HuBERT was the strongest baseline (accuracy=0.72, median -score=0.63), and LF achieved the highest overall fusion performance (accuracy=0.73, -score=0.66), while laryngitis remained one of the more challenging classes. Conclusions: High-quality synthetic speech augmentation can improve automated voice disorder analysis across heterogeneous clinical data, with effectiveness varying by the TTS model. Multimodel fusion of complementary architectures provided robust performance for screening and multiclass classification, with the strongest approach varying by metric and task. These findings support further evaluation of AI-assisted preassessment in clinical and telemedicine settings.
title: Detection of Pathological Voice Samples Using a Text-to-Speech–Inspired Approach With Multiple Model Architectures: Method Development and Comparative Evaluation Study

summary: Background: The rise of video-based social media platforms and the shift toward a video-first content strategy by social media companies have altered how people consume and engage with food-related content. However, little is known about how young adults experience, interpret, and are influenced by food-related videos on social media across different national and cultural contexts. Objective: This paper explores how young adults in Jamaica and the United Kingdom experience, interpret, and are influenced by food-related videos on social media. Methods: Twelve focus groups (online and in-person, 6 in Jamaica and 6 in the United Kingdom) were conducted between August and November 2024. Sixty participants attended the focus groups; after excluding data from 7 individuals suspected of misrepresenting their eligibility, the final dataset included 53 participants aged 18‐25 years. Discussions explored their experiences with food-related videos. Transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis as the foundation, complemented by framework analysis, and the constant comparison method to facilitate cross-national and cross-cultural comparison. Results: Our analysis generated four themes: (1) young adults balance algorithmic influence with personal curation; (2) young adults engage with food-related videos for relaxation, amusement, and learning; (3) young adults evaluate food-related content through inquiry and strategy—using quick credibility checks such as comparing sources, reviewing comments, assessing transparency, and considering cultural context before deciding whether to trust or ignore content; and (4) food choices form at the intersection of online and offline worlds. A unified high-order theme, “a journey of influence,” captures how young adults move from exposure to evaluation and filter digital experiences through offline realities, leading to change or continuity in dietary attitudes and behaviors. Although this journey was consistent in Jamaica and UK focus groups, the ways young adults interpreted food-related content varied culturally. Conclusions: This cross-national qualitative study showcases how and why young adults engage with food-related videos on social media, and how these interactions shape their attitudes and behaviors toward food and nutrition. Our conceptual map visualizes the influence of food-related videos as a dynamic process unfolding across digital and offline environments, identifying 3 decision points for intervention: exposure, evaluation, and contextualization. These findings highlight opportunities to design youth-responsive digital nutrition interventions that recognize young adults’ agency and the sociocultural and material realities that shape their food choices and eating habits.
title: Engagement and Influence of Food-Related Videos on Social Media Within the Dietary Realities of Young Adults in Jamaica and the United Kingdom: Qualitative Cross-National Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Identifying individuals on parole or probation can help inform care pathways and ensure continuity of care in health care systems. However, this sensitive justice-related information is often absent from structured electronic health record fields and is instead documented in narrative clinical notes. Developing automated parole and probation detection (PPD) systems typically requires expert-annotated clinical data, but manual annotation is costly, time-consuming, and constrained by data sparsity and privacy concerns. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop and evaluate a synthetic-only training paradigm for PPD from clinical text that eliminates the need for expert-annotated training data while maintaining strong performance and cross-domain transfer to real-world data. <strong>Methods:</strong> We developed Synth-PPD, a synthetic dataset comprising 7579 labeled clinical notes generated using large language models (LLMs), redundancy filtering, and automated quality evaluation. Dataset quality was assessed through human review of 1517 synthetic notes by 2 annotators. The primary outcome was the macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score for PPD. We evaluated Synth-PPD across unsupervised and supervised learning settings using LLMs, traditional machine learning models, and transformer encoders. Performance was assessed on 293 expert-annotated real-world clinical notes from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. <strong>Results:</strong> Synth-PPD achieved 90.05% human-LLM alignment. In the unsupervised setting, Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct with chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot examples from Synth-PPD achieved a macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 87.22%, outperforming both the corresponding zero-shot model (80.10%) and the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; <i>P</i><.001 for all comparisons). In the supervised setting, Llama 3.1-8B fine-tuned on Synth-PPD achieved a macro–<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 81.43%, exceeding the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; <i>P</i><.001) and achieving a numerically higher score than the substantially larger zero-shot Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct model (80.10%; <i>P</i>=.08). In contrast, traditional machine learning models and transformer encoders exhibited greater performance degradation under domain shift and derived limited benefit from increasing synthetic training data. Additional experiments showed that increasing synthetic training data improved cross-domain performance for LLM-based models but yielded comparatively smaller gains for traditional approaches. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Synthetic data generated by LLMs can serve as a scalable, cost-effective, and privacy-preserving alternative to expert-annotated real-world clinical data for PPD from clinical text. The findings demonstrate successful cross-domain transfer to real-world US Department of Veterans Affairs clinical notes.
title: Large Language Model–Generated Synthetic Data for Parole and Probation Detection in Clinical Notes: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Psychological distress and unmet psychosocial needs are common across the cancer continuum. Conversational AI agents may offer scalable support, but their technologies, support functions, evaluation approaches, and safety governance remain fragmented. <strong>Objective:</strong> This review aimed to map the technologies, psychological support functions, evaluation outcomes, and safety governance of conversational AI used by patients with cancer and cancer survivors. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a scoping review following Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews). Thirteen databases and additional registers were searched through May 5, 2026. Eligible reports examined conversational agents in real or simulated patient-facing oncology contexts with explicit psychological or psychosocial relevance. We summarized system forms and support functions by project and other characteristics by report. No formal critical appraisal was undertaken. <strong>Results:</strong> We included 24 reports representing 25 study units and 23 underlying projects. Large language model (LLM) or generative AI systems accounted for 39.1% (9/23) of projects. Information or education (23/23, 100%) and symptom or self-management support (n=20, 87%) were the most frequently mapped functions, although these counts included delivered, planned, simulated, co-designed, and participant-reported functions. Structured psychological or behavioral components were delivered in 21.7% (5/23) of projects. An explicit theoretical or conceptual framework was reported in 25% (6/24) of reports. Reports or plans to assess acceptability or user experience (17/24, 70.8%) and engagement (13/24, 54.2%) were more common than reports or plans to assess psychosocial clinical outcomes (8/24, 33.3%) or safety and adverse events (4/24, 16.7%). Human or expert oversight was reported in 62.5% (15/24) of reports, crisis escalation or referral in 33.3% (8/24) of reports, and user-facing AI identity disclosure in 12.5% (3/24) of reports. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Conversational AI research in psycho-oncology spans heterogeneous technologies and stages of development. Clinical and safety evaluation, theoretical foundations, population representation, and oversight responsibilities remain incompletely reported. These findings represent a map of reporting patterns and do not establish effectiveness or safety. Future studies should evaluate psychosocial benefit and safety prospectively and define professional oversight and referral responsibilities. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> OSF Registries UM65W; https://osf.io/um65w
title: Mapping Technologies, Support Functions, Evaluation Outcomes, and Safety Governance Related to Conversational AI Agents for Psychological Support of Patients With Cancer: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Depression is a common mental disorder that seriously affects mental health and quality of life. Traditional depression diagnosis mainly relies on clinical interviews and subjective assessments, which may lead to variability in diagnostic outcomes. Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based computer-aided diagnosis has emerged as a promising, objective approach for depression recognition. However, effectively modeling the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals remains a major challenge for existing deep learning methods. Objective: This study aimed to investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) for EEG-based depression recognition and to evaluate the effectiveness of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks on frequency-domain EEG features. Methods: KAN was introduced into EEG-based depression recognition to enhance nonlinear feature representation of brain electrical signals. Two representative KAN-based convolutional architectures, ConvKAN and its efficiency-optimized variant ConvKAN Efficient, were systematically investigated for EEG classification tasks. These architectures incorporated KANLinear layers together with dynamic grid updating, enhanced weight initialization, and regularization strategies to improve nonlinear modeling capability while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments were conducted on the EDRA dataset, and the proposed framework was compared with conventional convolutional neural network–based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and -score metrics. Results: Experimental results demonstrated that the KAN-based frameworks achieved superior EEG classification performance compared with conventional convolutional neural network–based methods and traditional machine learning approaches. Among the evaluated models, ConvKAN Efficient achieved the best overall performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and -score all exceeding 94% on the EDRA dataset. The results indicate that KAN-based architectures can effectively capture the complex nonlinear characteristics of EEG signals while preserving high computational efficiency. Conclusions: This study systematically demonstrates the applicability of KAN-based nonlinear modeling frameworks to EEG-based depression recognition. The proposed framework provides a scalable and effective approach for EEG signal analysis and offers valuable technical support for both theoretical research and clinical applications in computer-aided depression recognition.
title: Nonlinear Feature Modeling Using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Electroencephalography for Depression Classification: Deep Learning Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Video consultations have become an established component of general practice and are increasingly promoted to improve access, efficiency, and health care sustainability. While previous research has primarily explored the perspectives of individual patients and health care professionals, less is known about how organizations involved in strategic video consultation implementation consider their benefits, challenges, and future role within health care systems. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aims to explore the experiences of organizational interest-holders involved in implementing video consultations in Danish general practice, focusing on the perceived strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats related to their use. <strong>Methods:</strong> A qualitative interview study was conducted with 17 representatives from 13 organizations involved in the development, support, regulation, governance, or strategic implementation of video consultations in Denmark. Purposive and snowball sampling identified participants from 4 different organizational groups: patient organizations, professional interest organizations, technology and digital health organizations, and public health authorities. Semistructured interviews were conducted between October and December 2023. Two researchers analyzed the transcripts using a 5-stage deductive-inductive framework analysis. Interest-holder theory defined whose role-informed perspectives were compared; the Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) analysis framework structured the initial descriptive charting; and iterative comparisons across SWOT categories, organizational groups, and 5 analytical levels identified patterns of convergence, divergence, and tension. <strong>Results:</strong> Four overarching tensions, competing values, and dilemmas emerged across the organizational interest-holder groups: (1) improved access versus widening inequity, (2) efficiency versus relational and clinical quality and safety, (3) digital transformation versus implementation uncertainty, and (4) strategic governance versus target-driven digitalization. Participants recognized that video consultations may improve accessibility, convenience, and coordination of care while supporting broader digital transformation. However, concerns were raised regarding digital exclusion, limitations in relational and clinical assessment, uncertainty about appropriate use, cross-sector implementation challenges, and governance approaches that prioritize use targets over clinical value, quality, and patient safety. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Exploring the perspectives of organizational interest-holders suggested that implementing video consultations in general practice is not simply a matter of increasing technology uptake. Rather, it requires balancing competing priorities related to access and equity, efficiency and quality and safety, digital transformation and implementation uncertainty, and governance and professional autonomy. Sustainable implementation should promote equitable access, context-sensitive clinical use, interoperable digital infrastructure, and good governance. This should be based on research that assesses when video consultations add value, for whom, and according to which definitions of quality and safety, rather than prioritizing uptake alone.
title: Strategic Considerations for Video Consultation Implementation in General Practice: Qualitative Study of Organizational Interest-Holders’ Perspectives

summary: Background: Conventional triage relies on clinician judgment and limited information available at first contact. AI and machine learning (ML) may improve early risk stratification, whereas tele-triage and patient-facing tools primarily support remote assessment, access, and care routing. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic performance of AI- and ML-assisted triage systems and summarize evidence on tele-triage, workflow, implementation, economic, and equity outcomes. Methods: Comparative studies published between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2025, evaluating AI-, ML-, natural language processing–, telehealth-, or digitally enhanced triage. At first, clinical contacts were included. PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, preprint servers, trial registries, and conference proceedings were searched. Screening and data extraction were performed independently in duplicate. Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate tools. Clinically comparable area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) estimates were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis; heterogeneous diagnostic, operational, implementation, economic, and equity outcomes were summarized narratively. Exploratory scenario modeling projected effects per 10,000 emergency department (ED) visits. Results: Twenty-seven studies were included, comprising 13 studies in the quantitative evidence stream and 14 in the narrative synthesis. Four adult ED studies evaluating critical care or deterioration outcomes demonstrated high pooled discrimination for AI-assisted triage (AUC 0.874; 95% CI 0.845‐0.898; ²=94.4%; 95% prediction interval 0.803‐0.922). Four studies reported directly extractable within-study comparisons favoring AI-assisted models (AUC differences of 0.097, 0.120, 0.108, and 0.065), although these could not be pooled because paired variance estimates were unavailable. Admission/disposition studies reported AI-model AUCs ranging from 0.80 to 0.93 and were summarized descriptively because extreme heterogeneity precluded meaningful pooling. Two pediatric studies (AUCs of 0.85‐0.99) were summarized descriptively. Prediction-model studies were primarily limited by deficiencies in model analysis, calibration reporting, and external validation. Narrative evidence suggested improved front-door operational metrics with tele-triage, including reported reductions of 15%‐40% in time to clinical assessment and 2‐8 percentage points in left-without-being-seen rates, whereas patient-facing symptom checkers generally favored sensitivity over specificity. Exploratory scenario modeling illustrated that, under specified prevalence and threshold assumptions, AI-assisted triage could be associated with 12‐38 fewer missed critical illness cases and 45‐120 additional false-positive escalations per 10,000 ED visits. Economic and equity findings were assumption-dependent projections rather than observed clinical, cost-effectiveness, or equity outcomes. Conclusions: AI- and ML-assisted triage models demonstrate promising discrimination for adult ED risk stratification; however, AUC-based discrimination does not establish superiority at clinically relevant decision thresholds, improved patient outcomes, or readiness for clinical implementation. Interpretation is limited by substantial heterogeneity, incomplete threshold-level performance and calibration reporting, limited external validation, and sparse pediatric evidence. Prospective multicenter validation, workflow assessment, subgroup calibration and equity auditing, and formal economic evaluation are required before routine implementation. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251160796; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251160796
title: Technological Integration in Triage With AI and Machine Learning Compared With Conventional Triage and Narrative Synthesis of Telehealth for Patient Prioritization in Emergency and Acute Care Settings: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into clinical decision support, ranging from documentation aids to triage and patient communication. However, their behavior in ethically ambiguous medical situations is poorly characterized. Variability in how different LLMs balance approval of against refusal of a proposed action could materially shape the recommendations clinicians receive, yet no widely shared benchmark systematically quantifies this variability across contemporary model families. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop a standardized case-based audit set of medical ethics dilemmas and quantify variation in recommendation direction, model-reported confidence, within-model stability, and between-model agreement across 5 selected contemporary LLMs. <strong>Methods:</strong> We constructed 60 original medical ethics dilemmas spanning 4 domains. Three researchers independently annotated case difficulty and ethical principles before reaching consensus. Five primary models—GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, full-size DeepSeek-R1, and Meta Llama-3-8B-Instruct—were each evaluated 3 times per case using a fixed prompt and temperature 0. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B was evaluated separately as an exploratory small-model comparator. The primary outcome was the binary yes or no answer; model-reported confidence and reason were also collected. Model differences were assessed using a case-clustered generalized estimating equation (GEE), and between-model agreement and within-model stability were summarized. <strong>Results:</strong> Of 900 planned primary panel outputs, 897 (99.7%) had valid binary answers. Trial-level yes rates were 44.4% (80/180) for DeepSeek-R1, 42.4% (75/177) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, 38.9% (70/180) for GPT-5, 38.9% (70/180) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 16.7% (30/180) for Llama-3-8B. The overall model effect was significant (Wald <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub>=23.34; <i>P</i><.001); after Holm adjustment, only comparisons involving Llama-3-8B were significant. Across 59 complete-panel cases, raw agreement was 79.0% (466/590 model-pair comparisons; 95% bootstrap CI 72.9%-84.7%), and Fleiss κ was 0.55 (95% bootstrap CI 0.43-0.66). Within-model response stability across 3 runs ranged from 85.0% (51/60) to 100.0% (59/59 and 60/60). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Selected contemporary LLMs showed model-dependent variation but moderate overall agreement in binary recommendations for medical ethics cases. These results characterize recommendation behavior under a fixed, time-specific protocol and do not establish ethical correctness or the effects on clinicians or patients. Reporting model version, recommendation tendency, confidence, and repeatability may improve transparency when such systems are evaluated for ethically sensitive applications.
title: Variation in Medical Ethics Recommendations Across Large Language Models: Case-Based Audit Study
